blogs.title: When Threats Fall Short: Jimenez v. Bondi and the Tenth Circuit’s Reassessed Standard for Past Persecution
blogs.description: The court’s refusal to equate a series of phone calls and a warning brochure with "past persecution" is a stark reminder that the asylum bar continues to demand harder evidence of actual harm.  This post examines how Judge Tymkovich reiterates the distinction between "expressions of fear" and "mark upon the mind" that breach the INA’s threshold, how the decision fits into the wave of cases that have tightened the requirement for threats alone, and what it means for Latin American applicants who rely on a pattern of intimidation rather than physical violence to justify their refugee status.

blogs.title: Safe in the Homeland? The Tenth Circuit’s Narrow Safe Relocation Doctrine in Jimenez v. Bondi
blogs.description: Jimenez v. Bondi is a textbook analysis of what it takes to satisfy the safe‑relocation prong of the asylum and withholding framework.  We dissect the court’s insistence on a “well‑documented knowledge” of government failure, the deference given to the applicant’s limited attempts to report past persecution, and how the availability of a family in the countryside failed to offset a failure to prove a protected category.  The post also compares the 10th Circuit’s treatment with other circuits, illuminating a flexible but stringent approach that may shape future internal‑relocation arguments for Colombian and other Latin American asylum seekers.

blogs.title: The Substantial Evidence Standard in Action: How Jimenez v. Bondi Reaffirms Judicial Deference in Asylum Appeals
blogs.description: While the appeal was denied, the opinion is a lodestar of how the 10th Circuit applies the "substantial‑evidence" standard to BIA findings.  This piece reviews the court’s insistence that it will not "re‑weigh the evidence" but merely decide whether a reasonable adjudicator could find the same conclusion.  It explores the implications for immigration practitioners who routinely argue that BIA findings are “clearly erroneous” and how the opinion sharpens the line between appellate review and deference in asylum cases.

blogs.title: Political Opinion and Mixed Motive Harassment: The Tenth Circuit’s Tightened Nexus Requirement in Jimenez v. Bondi
blogs.description: By ruling that Jimenez’s persecution was “tangential” to his political affiliation, the court refines the nexus standard for asylum on the grounds of political opinion.  The post deconstructs the court’s analysis of a "central reason," contrasts the decision with earlier 10th Circuit precedent that accepted a secondary motive, and outlines the strategic implications for attorneys representing politically active refugees, especially those whose persecution may be intertwined with criminal or paramilitary actors.
